q: Fatima's textile sales drop every rainy season, so she starts making waterproof bags. Which strategy is she using?
a: Cutting costs during a slow season
Selling something that peaks when sales dip
Offering subscriptions to smooth her income
Building a reserve during strong months
quote: Develop complementary products or services that sell when your main offerings slow down. Fatima developed waterproof bags that sell especially well during the rainy season, balancing her annual cash flow.

q: Three new vendors open near Samuel's stall and undercut his prices. What does the chapter suggest he do?
a: Match their prices to keep his regulars.
Lower his quality slightly to cut costs.
Move his stall to a less crowded spot.
Add extras like delivery and cooking tips.
quote: Samuel in Kenya stopped competing on price. Instead, he began offering free delivery for regular customers and providing cooking suggestions with each purchase.

q: Elena is worn out from cleaning, scheduling, and talking with customers. Which change follows the chapter's advice?
a: Hand scheduling to a low-cost helper
Add new services to raise her income
Work longer days during busy weeks
Hire a manager to run the business
quote: Find low-cost help for time-consuming but simple activities. Elena hired her teenage nephew to handle customer scheduling.

q: Carlos worries that his food stall doesn't meet all the rules. What approach does the chapter recommend?
a: Avoid inspectors until he is fully registered.
Pay for full registration right away.
Ask a health inspector for advice.
Move to a market with fewer rules.
quote: He built a relationship with a local health inspector, asking for advice rather than avoiding contact.

q: Ahmed does carpentry for homeowners, small shops, a hotel, and government offices. Which kind of diversification is this?
a: Product
Location
Seasonal
Customer
quote: Customer diversification: Develop multiple customer segments to avoid dependence on any single group. When economic conditions affected one customer segment, others sustained his business.

q: Priya sells at a village stall, through city shops, at a tourist market, and on WhatsApp. What does this mainly protect her from?
a: Losing income when one sales spot has problems
Competitors copying her best-selling products
Running short of materials in busy months
Paying higher taxes as her sales grow
quote: When one location experienced problems (like weather affecting the market), other channels maintained her income.

q: How should a small business think about formalization?
a: As a yes-or-no choice made once at the start
As a step required before making any sales
As a series of levels to climb as it grows
As a task only for businesses with employees
quote: Rather than seeing formalization as a yes/no decision, view it as a spectrum with multiple levels.

q: A tailor joins the local market association and pays the standard stall fee. Which formalization level is this?
a: Basic safety and community standards
Local recognition
Partial formalization
Full formalization
quote: Level 2, Local Recognition: A tailor registering with the local market association and paying standard fees for their stall.

q: Which of these is a benefit of formalizing a business?
a: Lower overall tax payments
Less record-keeping each month
Fewer rules to follow
The chance to serve larger clients
quote: Benefits of increased formalization include the Ability to serve larger customers who require documentation.

q: Elena's cleaning service has five employees, and formalizing worries her because of the cost. What did she do?
a: Registered everything at once to avoid penalties
Stayed informal until the costs came down
Registered the business, then workers one at a time
Registered her workers first, then the business
quote: She formalized gradually, first registering the business while learning about labor requirements, then formally registering employees one by one as revenue from new corporate clients increased.

q: A home food producer can't afford formal certification yet. What should she focus on first?
a: Saving until she can pay for certification
Following real safety practices and writing them down
Waiting until an inspector visits her kitchen
Getting the paperwork in order before anything else
quote: Focus first on actual safety practices, not just compliance paperwork. Document your safety procedures, even in simple form.

q: A furniture maker runs his workshop from home. How can he avoid trouble with neighbors?
a: Keep set hours and control the dust.
Move into a rented shop right away.
Work late when neighbors are away.
Register as a formal business first.
quote: The furniture maker maintained strict working hours and dust control to accommodate neighbors.

q: An inspector visits Maria's production space, which isn't fully up to standard yet. What's her best approach?
a: Say it already meets every requirement.
Close until the space fully complies.
Ask a friend to speak for her instead.
Show a written plan for gradual fixes.
quote: Progressive compliance: She showed him her written plan for gradually improving the facility. He allowed her to continue operating while implementing improvements on an agreed timeline.

q: Street vendors want set vending areas and simpler permits from the city. What's most likely to work?
a: Each vendor applies for a permit alone
The vendors form an association together
The vendors hire a lawyer to fight the city
Each vendor moves to a less-watched area
quote: Street vendors in a Colombian city formed an association that successfully negotiated with municipal authorities for designated vending areas and simplified permit processes that individual vendors couldn't have achieved alone.

q: Jasmine's skincare sales are strong some weeks and almost zero in others. What did she do?
a: Cut her prices to draw steady buyers
Took a loan to cover the slow weeks
Created monthly subscription packages
Stopped selling individual products
quote: She analyzed her sales patterns and created a subscription model where customers received monthly product packages. This created reliable base income.
